title: Paper 1 style practice: Sabr Cycles
subject: Business

intro: Read the case. Answer every part in the spaces, then start the 12-mark evaluation (finish it in the portal box). Use the case in every answer.

passage.title: Sabr Cycles
paras: Sabr Cycles is a bicycle repair shop owned by Idris, a sole trader. He opened it four years ago in a market town. He repairs about 150 bikes a month, charging an average of £45 a repair. Parts and other variable costs average £15 a repair; rent, insurance and his assistant's wages come to £3,600 a month.
Business is seasonal: busy from April to September, quiet in winter. Last winter Idris ran short of cash and paid a supplier late, and the supplier now asks for payment before delivery.

Electric bikes are becoming popular in the town. Idris is thinking about selling new e-bikes as well as repairing them. Each e-bike would cost him £1,200 and sell for £1,600. He would need to buy 10 to display, and train on e-bike repairs (£900 course).
passage.source: All businesses, people and figures in this case are fictional, made up for practice.

questions.a: Costs that do not change with output (B1)

questions.q: (b) Calculate Sabr Cycles' break-even number of repairs a month.
(c) Explain one advantage to Idris of being a sole trader.
questions.a: He makes all the decisions himself (point), so he can respond quickly, e.g. to e-bike demand (development), and keeps all the profit (development)

questions.q: (d) Analyse the effects on Sabr Cycles of its cash-flow problem last winter.
questions.a: Paid a supplier late, so the supplier now wants payment before delivery: Idris needs cash before he can repair bikes, making winter cash flow worse; he may lose trade credit, so he must keep more cash or borrow. Level 3 (5-6): a balanced analysis with two developed chains of reasoning, both in context. Level 2 (3-4): developed reasoning, partly in context. Level 1 (1-2): points identified with little development.

questions.q: (e) Evaluate whether Sabr Cycles should start selling new e-bikes. (Start here; finish in the portal box.)
questions.a: For: profit of £400 an e-bike; growing demand; repairs of e-bikes later. Against: 10 bikes cost £12,000 of stock plus £900 training, a large outflow for a business that ran short of cash, and the supplier wants payment up front. Judgement: e.g. start with fewer bikes or order to customer demand; it depends on how fast they sell. Level 4 (10-12): developed chains of reasoning on both sides in context, and a supported judgement with 'it depends on'. Level 3 (7-9): both sides developed, judgement partly supported. Level 2 (4-6): some development, one-sided or generic. Level 1 (1-3): points identified.
